ACWR

Overview

The ACWR package has been designed to calculate the acute chronic workload ratio using three different methods: exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA), rolling average coupled (RAC) and rolling average uncoupled (RAU).

Sessions are placed on a daily calendar: sessions on the same day are summed and days without a session count as a load of 0. Acute and chronic loads are then computed over calendar days, not over sessions:

  • Acute load: sum of the daily load over the last 7 days.
  • RAC chronic load: sum over the last 28 days / 4 (coupled).
  • RAU chronic load: sum over days 8 to 28 before today / 3 (uncoupled).
  • EWMA: exponentially weighted moving averages with time-decay constants of 7 and 28 days, updated every calendar day (Williams et al., 2017).

Version 0.2.0 fixed a bug: results of earlier versions are only correct when there was exactly one session every day. See NEWS.md.

Resources

  • Application of ACWR: Gabbett TJ (2016). The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? British Journal of Sports Medicine, 50(5), 273-280. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-095788
  • Rolling average method: Windt J, Gabbett TJ (2019). Is it all for naught? What does mathematical coupling mean for acute:chronic workload ratios? British Journal of Sports Medicine, 53(16), 988-990. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-098925
  • Exponentially weighted moving averages method: Williams S, West S, Cross MJ, Stokes KA (2017). Better way to determine the acute:chronic workload ratio? British Journal of Sports Medicine, 51(3), 209-210. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096589; and Murray NB, Gabbett TJ, Townshend AD (2017). Calculating acute:chronic workload ratios using exponentially weighted moving averages provides a more sensitive indicator of injury likelihood than rolling averages. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 51(9), 749-754. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-097152

Example

This is a basic example which shows you how to use the ACWR package:

install.packages("ACWR")
library(ACWR)

First, we have to load the data stored in the package. training_load has one session every day; training_load_rest has rest days, a day with two sessions and a week without training.

data("training_load", package = "ACWR")
data("training_load_rest", package = "ACWR")

Then, we can calculate the ACWR:

result_ACWR <- ACWR(db = training_load_rest,
                    ID = "ID",
                    TL = "TL",
                    days = "Day",
                    training_dates = "Training_Date",
                    ACWR_method = c("EWMA", "RAC", "RAU"))

RAC and RAU are NA until 28 days of history exist. Use partial = TRUE to use the days available instead.

Additionally, individual plots can be obtained:

ACWR_plot <- plot_ACWR(db = result_ACWR,
                       TL = "TL",
                       ACWR = "RAC_ACWR",
                       day = "Day",
                       ID = "ID")

Functions for each individual method have been implemented too:

# Select the first subject
training_load_1 <- training_load_rest[training_load_rest[["ID"]] == 1, ]

# EWMA
result_EWMA <- EWMA(TL = training_load_1$TL,
                    training_dates = training_load_1$Training_Date)

# RAC
result_RAC <- RAC(TL = training_load_1$TL,
                  training_dates = training_load_1$Training_Date)

# RAU
result_RAU <- RAU(TL = training_load_1$TL,
                  training_dates = training_load_1$Training_Date)

Limitations of the ACWR

The package calculates the ACWR as it is described in the literature, but the ratio has well-documented limitations that should be considered before using it to make decisions:

  • Mathematical coupling. In the coupled ratio, the acute week is also part of the chronic load, which creates a spurious correlation between the two and reduces the between-athlete variability of the chronic load (Lolli et al., 2019); the coupled ratio can never exceed 4 (Windt & Gabbett, 2019). The uncoupled ratio removes the overlap, but not the other problems below.
  • Ratio artefacts. The ACWR behaves as a rescaling of the acute load: similar associations with injury are obtained when the acute load is divided by fixed or random “chronic” loads, and the ratio adds no predictive value over the acute load alone (Impellizzeri et al., 2021). A ratio may not always be an appropriate way to represent changes in activity, and EWMA values depend on the initial load in the first weeks (Wang et al., 2020).
  • No validated thresholds. Recommended ACWR thresholds (e.g. a “sweet spot” of 0.8-1.3) are affected by these limitations and by problems such as discretization and sparse data, which undermine their validity as cut-offs for injury risk (Wang et al., 2020; Impellizzeri et al., 2021).

References:

  • Lolli L, Batterham AM, Hawkins R, et al. (2019). Mathematical coupling causes spurious correlation within the conventional acute-to-chronic workload ratio calculations. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 53(15), 921-922. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-098110
  • Impellizzeri FM, Woodcock S, Coutts AJ, et al. (2021). What role do chronic workloads play in the acute to chronic workload ratio? Time to dismiss ACWR and its underlying theory. Sports Medicine, 51(3), 581-592. doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01378-6
  • Wang C, Vargas JT, Stokes T, et al. (2020). Analyzing activity and injury: lessons learned from the acute:chronic workload ratio. Sports Medicine, 50(7), 1243-1254. doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01280-1
